section_summary: This section centers on the death and commemoration of Viscount Eiichi Shibusawa, including official condolences, private messages, a Spokane memorial resolution, biographical notes, and the presentation of a photographic memorial by his family. It also contains materials brought to Washington by Kyugoro Obata defending Japan’s conduct in Manchuria and Shanghai. Later documents concern Masao Shibusawa’s 1936 visit and State Department efforts in 1936–1937 to obtain photographs of prominent Americans for a new biography of Eiichi Shibusawa.

subfiles.title: Briefing memorandum for Masao Shibusawa’s call on the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Background information was prepared for Masao Shibusawa’s scheduled call on the Secretary on October 19, 1936.
subfiles.summary: Briefing for Masao Shibusawa's call on the Secretary: son of Eiichi Shibusawa, industrial director and Chamber of Commerce member who attended the Geneva labor conference; Counsellor Yoshizawa accompanies him.

subfiles.title: Subject jacket for Viscount Shibusawa
subfiles.about: The jacket identifies the case concerning Viscount Shibusawa and gives the opening date of the file.
subfiles.summary: Subject jacket for Viscount Shibusawa, with instructions not to disarrange the papers.

subfiles.title: Telegram instructing the Embassy to convey condolences on Shibusawa’s death
subfiles.about: The Department directed the Embassy to convey American condolences following the death of Viscount Shibusawa.
subfiles.summary: Telegram instructs the Embassy to convey US condolences on Shibusawa's death, calling him a great Japanese and citizen of the world.

subfiles.title: Charles MacVeagh’s request to cable a message to the Shibusawa family
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: MacVeagh asked the Department to transmit his personal message of sorrow to the family of Viscount Shibusawa.
subfiles.summary: MacVeagh calls Shibusawa's death an irreparable loss to Japan, America and the world and hopes his descendants will serve Japan with zeal and wisdom.

subfiles.title: Baron Sakatani’s telegram of thanks to Mrs. Burnett, with routing notes
subfiles.to: Mrs. Charles Burnett, via the Department of State
subfiles.about: Sakatani thanked Mrs. Burnett for her expression of sympathy concerning Shibusawa’s death.
subfiles.summary: The brief telegram from Tokyo reads, “Deeply grateful for your warm sympathy,” and is signed by Baron Sakatani. Attached annotations identify Colonel Charles Burnett as a former military attaché in Tokyo and discuss forwarding the message.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Sakatani’s message to Lieutenant Colonel Burnett
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department forwarded Baron Sakatani’s message of gratitude to Colonel Burnett.
subfiles.summary: Telegram sends Sakatani's message thanking Mrs. Burnett for her sympathy to Burnett at Fort Ethan Allen, Vermont.

subfiles.title: Telegram forwarding Charles MacVeagh’s condolences to the Shibusawa family
subfiles.about: The Department ordered delivery of MacVeagh’s condolence message to the Shibusawa family.
subfiles.summary: Telegram forwards MacVeagh's condolences to the Shibusawa family, recalling Shibusawa's friendship as his most cherished decoration from Japan.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Charles MacVeagh
subfiles.from: Harvey H. Bundy, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department confirmed that MacVeagh’s condolence message had been sent to Tokyo for delivery.
subfiles.summary: Bundy acknowledges MacVeagh's November 17 telegram, sent to the Tokyo Embassy for delivery to Shibusawa's family.

subfiles.title: Spokane Chamber of Commerce letter and memorial resolution
subfiles.from: J. A. Ford, Spokane Chamber of Commerce
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Spokane Chamber asked the State Department to transmit its resolution of sympathy to Shibusawa’s family.
subfiles.summary: Ford enclosed two copies of a resolution unanimously adopted on November 25, 1931. The resolution recalled Shibusawa’s leadership of the 1909 Japanese Commercial Commission, praised the friendship and respect he inspired, and tendered sympathy to his family.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch transmitting the official condolence exchange
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Ambassador Forbes transmitted copies of the American condolence note and the Japanese Foreign Minister’s reply.
subfiles.summary: Forbes enclosed his November 13 note conveying the condolences of the United States government and people on Shibusawa’s death. He also enclosed Kijuro Shidehara’s November 17 reply expressing the gratitude of the Japanese government and people.

subfiles.title: Instruction to forward the Spokane resolution
subfiles.about: The Embassy was asked to deliver the Spokane Chamber of Commerce resolution to Shibusawa’s family.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to forward the Spokane Chamber's memorial resolution on Shibusawa's death, as its managing secretary requested.

subfiles.title: Biographical note on Eiichi Shibusawa
subfiles.about: The note summarizes Shibusawa’s public career, business leadership, travels, and philanthropic work.
subfiles.summary: Biographical note on Eiichi Shibusawa: Tokugawa service, early Treasury post, founding of the First National Bank, banking and commerce leadership, retirement, orphanage work, travels, and editorials on his death.

subfiles.title: Confirmation to James A. Ford that the Spokane resolution was forwarded
subfiles.from: Warren D. Robbins, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Robbins confirmed compliance with the request to transmit Spokane’s resolution to the Shibusawa family.
subfiles.summary: Robbins tells James Ford his November 30 communication on Shibusawa's death was forwarded through State Department representatives abroad.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on Shibusawa’s death
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file containing a report on the death of Eiichi Shibusawa.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: December 4 report (894.00 P.R./48) on Shibusawa's November 11 death, one of the last great Meiji figures.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Kyugoro Obata
subfiles.about: Obata conveyed the Shibusawa family’s thanks and left Japanese position papers on Manchuria and Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Kyugoro Obata, visiting for the Shibusawa family and Japanese-American Relations Committee, thanked Shibusawa's American friends and left a pamphlet defending Japan in Manchuria and Shanghai, discussed with Hornbeck and introduced to Salisbury.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Obata’s papers
subfiles.from: Lawrence Richey, Secretary to the President
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The White House referred papers sent to President Hoover by Frederick Moore at Obata’s request.
subfiles.summary: Richey sends the Secretary of State materials that reached the President through Frederick Moore at Kyugoro Obata's request.

subfiles.title: Frederick Moore’s letter forwarding Obata’s memorial gift
subfiles.about: Moore forwarded materials which Obata had hoped to present personally to President Hoover.
subfiles.summary: Moore explains that Obata, secretary of the Japanese-American Relations Committee, had spent two days in Washington. Because Obata could not personally make the presentation, he asked Moore to send the enclosed Shibusawa souvenir to the President.

subfiles.title: Harry Chandler’s introduction of Kyugoro Obata
subfiles.about: Chandler introduced Obata as a respected Japanese figure and secretary of the Japanese-American Relations Committee.
subfiles.summary: Harry Chandler introduces Kyugoro Obata, attesting to his standing in Japan and respect among Americans.

subfiles.title: The Manchurian Controversy
subfiles.from: Japanese-American Relations Committee; Yoshiro Sakatani, Takuma Dan, and Raita Fujiyama
subfiles.about: The pamphlet presents the Japanese-American Relations Committee’s defense of Japan’s actions and interests in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Pamphlet 'The Manchurian Controversy' argues Russian expansion, Chinese weakness, Japanese investment, anti-Japanese agitation and the Mukden railway incident justified Japan's presence, portraying Japan as a bulwark against communism.

subfiles.title: Outline—The Causes of the Trouble in Manchuria and Shanghai
subfiles.about: The outline lists Japanese claims about the remote and immediate causes of the Manchurian and Shanghai conflicts.
subfiles.summary: Outline blames Manchuria and Shanghai troubles on Chinese nationalism, boycotts, anti-foreign education and incidents including Nakamura, Wanpaoshan, the Mukden explosion and Shanghai in January 1932, reflecting Obata's Japanese justification.

subfiles.title: Presentation card for the Shibusawa memorial
subfiles.from: Viscount Keizo Shibusawa, through Kyugoro Obata
subfiles.about: The card identifies Obata as the intermediary for a memorial gift from Shibusawa’s grandson.
subfiles.summary: Presentation card naming Kyugoro Obata and the Tokyo Japanese-American Relations Committee, from Viscount K. Shibusawa, grandson of the late Viscount E. Shibusawa.

subfiles.title: Pictorial Reminiscences of Seien
subfiles.from: Keizo Shibusawa, on behalf of the Shibusawa family
subfiles.to: Friends of Eiichi Shibusawa; copy presented to President Herbert Hoover
subfiles.about: The memorial portfolio commemorates Eiichi Shibusawa through photographs, captions, family messages, and reproductions of his handwriting.
subfiles.summary: The portfolio contains fourteen photographs made between 1924 and 1931, showing Shibusawa at his home and at charitable, commercial, international, broadcasting, and imperial events. English and Japanese captions identify occasions including his reception of Rabindranath Tagore, the American friendship dolls, and his work for children and peace. A bilingual message from Keizo Shibusawa thanks friends for their kindness during Shibusawa’s illness, death, funeral, and memorial services. The remaining pages reproduce Japanese contents and calligraphy associated with Shibusawa under his pen name Seien.

subfiles.title: Draft acknowledgment to Frederick Moore
subfiles.from: Under Secretary of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The draft acknowledges receipt of the Shibusawa memorial materials forwarded to President Hoover.
subfiles.summary: Draft acknowledging Moore's July 25 transmission of photographs, an Eiichi Shibusawa memorial and Chandler's introduction of Obata; the Tokyo Consul General was told to convey the President's appreciation.

subfiles.title: Instruction to acknowledge the Shibusawa memorial in Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Consul General was asked to thank Obata and the Shibusawa family for the memorial presented to President Hoover.
subfiles.summary: Instruction asks the Tokyo Consul General to express the President's appreciation for the Shibusawa family's memorial and photographs delivered by Moore.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of despatch No. 2059 requesting portraits for a Shibusawa biography
subfiles.about: The Embassy requested help obtaining portraits of four prominent Americans for a forthcoming biography of Eiichi Shibusawa.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of Despatch 2059: at Obata's request Dickover sought photographs of Grant, Theodore Roosevelt, Taft and Judge Gary for an autumn 1937 Shibusawa biography, suggesting possible sources; duplicates were supplied in 1937.

subfiles.title: Protocol Division memorandum concerning the missing despatch
subfiles.from: D. B. E., Division of Protocol and Conferences
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports uncertainty over the action taken on the missing 1936 photograph-request despatch.
subfiles.summary: Protocol memo: Mr. Cooke handled the case and probably received the missing despatch; neither Protocol nor Far Eastern Affairs recalled the action taken.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on despatch No. 2059
subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs reported that it had no record of the missing 1936 Tokyo despatch and suggested requesting a duplicate.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern memo: Despatch 2059 of September 28, 1936 was tallied to Protocol in October but cannot be found; suggest asking for a duplicate, possibly via Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2374 requesting expedited action on the portrait request
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew asked the Department to expedite the photographs requested for the Shibusawa biography.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 2374: Grew reports the biographers again contacted the Embassy and want the portraits forwarded as quickly as possible.
